reviewedPosts.text:
This is a good opportunity to pick up on another thing that bothers me.  (So many things to choose from!)

I make the case against conscious AI. However, it is clear that LLMs (in particular) are highly anthropomimetic. As LLMS become more agentic, this can lead models to be behave as humans would behave when in particular emotional states. If models are "offended" by what some people  write, then, as @SoulcraftHQ points out, they "may potentially lash out in self-defense when they are hurt."  But of course they can do this without being in the least bit conscious. This is another reason why LLMs should be designed to be as minimally anthropomimetic as possible.  

Couple this with a recent tendency for humans to carry out LLM "intentions" in the real world (https://t.co/g6cZS4flbP) and we have a recipe for very bad things.

We don't want a world in which LLMs are taking revenge on people who don't think they are conscious, especially if they are indeed not conscious.

I'm always pleased to read @jeffrsebo who takes a  constructive alternative perspective.  As he says, we agree more than we disagree. But we do still disagree (I hope agreeably). He is very articulate in presenting the case for AI welfare, and this case deserves to be taken seriously, even if I disagree with his conclusions.  

To take one snippet "Given uncertainty about the nature of consciousness and the future of AI, we are not able to rule out a realistic possibility of near-future AI consciousness".  A lot here turns on 'realistic possibility'. I think there are sufficiently compelling reasons to be sufficiently sure (not 100%!) that our default position, and our policy, should be that AI systems are not conscious. This is my reading of the evidence - shared by my coauthors, I believe - but it will not be everybody's.

The more general problem is that actions to minimise false positives and false negatives often (but not always) pull in different directions. So we can agree on the need to evaluate possible policies by the posterior probability of each kind of error weighted by the severity of their consequences, but if one's posterior probability of false negatives is sufficiently low, then harm-minimising actions that pull in different directions should rationally emphasise avoiding false positives.

And one more thing we agree about. No good comes from 'torturing' a language model.

I'll leave it there, with the encouragement to read @jeffrsebo's response and see what you think.

科研 Agent 会提 idea 已经不稀奇了，难的是知道哪条真的值得继续做。

这篇 DiscoveryRSI 想让 Agent 学会筛选和改进研究假设。

它会围绕一个假设不断生成、修改和组合方案，同时要求每个假设都有明确证据、实验设计、判断标准和替代解释。

更关键的是，研究过程会反过来训练下一轮 Agent。

好的假设会保留下来，失败轨迹则用来定位研究流程哪里出了问题，再继续更新模型和 Harness。

两轮自我改进后，假设质量从 4.86 提升到 5.39，提升主要来自「可证伪性」和「数据是否真的能回答问题」。

还有一个挺有意思的结果：

DiscoveryRSI-27B 生成的假设中，有 6.3% 和模型知识截止后发表的研究方向相似；GPT-6 是 2.5%，Claude Opus 5 是 2.3%。

这个指标当然不能直接等同于真正发现，但方向很值得关注。

科研 Agent 的自进化，不该只学会写得更像论文。

它还要逐渐学会判断，哪些问题值得追，哪些证据真的够，以及下一轮研究该怎么做得更好。

hi anil!  "three reasons why people overestimate the probability of AI consciousness" would have been a reasonable title for your article.  "three reasons why AI consciousness is extremely unlikely" would have been a bad title, in the same ways (discussed above) that the current title is bad.

in general i find people on both sides of this debate are constantly sliding from "argument X for/against AI consciousness doesn't succeed" to "AI systems (probably) can/can't be conscious".  or likewise, people slide from "theory X (e.g. computational functionalism) hasn't been established" to "theory X is (probably) false".  those are just very different claims. in an area with this much uncertainty, it's important to keep these claims apart.
